earth_rotates_through_both_bulges_in_2: In an idealized ocean, rotation produces two tidal highs and lows per lunar day (about 24 h 50 min). Real coasts can have one, two unequal, or two similar highs; local timing and height depend on the basin and weather.
tf_phase_help: Choose the Moon–Sun angle at hour zero. Changing it restarts model time. The Moon keeps moving as you explore the next 48 hours.
tf_distance_help: These presets use NASA mean perigee, semimajor-axis and apogee distances. The chosen distance stays fixed during the 48-hour model.
tf_time_help: The sample point rotates once per solar day. The Moon moves too, producing a lunar day of about 24 h 50 min. Arrow keys move half an hour; Shift moves 2.5 hours.
tf_moon_status: Moon-only experiment: solar forcing is omitted.
tf_spring_status: Near spring alignment: lunar and solar contributions reinforce the largest spatial variation.
tf_neap_status: Near neap alignment: lunar and solar contributions partly cancel, reducing the spatial variation.
tf_transition_status: Between spring and neap alignments: the combined pattern changes as the Moon moves.
tf_legend: Cyan: Moon. Yellow dashed: Sun. Green: combined. Gold dot: the sample location.
tf_intro: Explore why the Sun and Moon produce spring and neap tides. The diagrams show an idealized tidal-forcing pattern and a sample point rotating through it. Values are relative to the Moon at its mean distance; they do not show local sea level.
tf_geometry_desc: View above the orbital plane. The Sun is to the right. Cyan and yellow outlines show the separate contributions; the green outline combines them. Sizes, orbit spacing and bulges are exaggerated.
tf_geometry_help: Diagram sizes and tidal bulges are exaggerated. The orbit spacing stays fixed on screen; the distance control changes the strength. The Moon icon is lit on the side facing the Sun.
tf_chart_title: Forcing at the rotating sample point
tf_chart_a11y: Select elapsed time on the tidal-forcing graph
tf_chart_desc: The two daily contributions add at every time. The vertical line and green point mark the selected time. Values are relative forcing, not water height.
tf_chart_help: Tap or drag on the graph to select model time. The lunar and solar curves have different periods. Green is their sum; the fixed vertical scale makes spring and neap cases comparable.
tf_current_forcing: Combined forcing at the sample point
tf_explanation: Why the two contributions behave this way
tf_explanation_body: Tides depend on the change in gravity across Earth. The leading tidal term scales as GM / distance³, so moving the Moon closer increases its contribution. The two opposite lobes produce the twice-per-lunar-day pattern in this coplanar model.
tf_local_limits: Real coasts can have one, two unequal, or two similar highs per day. Ocean depth, coast shape, latitude, friction and weather affect timing and water level. This model omits those effects.
tf_local_link: NOAA · Local tide observations and predictions
tf_source_basis: The gravitational parameters use JPL DE440 values. Both are converted to km³/s² before forming their ratio. NASA provides the reference lunar distances. A 29.53059-day mean synodic month and a 24-hour solar day set the model rates; the Moon distance is held constant. The reference values are embedded, so the explorer works offline.
tf_table_caption: Reference inputs used in the forcing ratio. GM is the gravitational parameter; distance is center to center. Solar GM is converted to km³/s² and rounded for display.
tf_math_limits: q is the varying part of an idealized equatorial tidal term, normalized to the mean-distance lunar contribution. The diagram and graph use the same q. The Moon–Sun angle advances with model time; the sample point starts on the sunward side of Earth. Inclination, eccentricity, ocean response, delays and measurement uncertainty are omitted.
